related_questions.question: Can federal employees keep their life insurance after retirement?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, federal employees can generally keep their Federal Employees' Group Life Insurance (FEGLI) coverage into retirement, but certain conditions must be met. To continue coverage, employees typically need to have been enrolled in FEGLI for the five years immediately preceding retirement, or for the full period of their federal service if less than five years, and they must retire on an immediate annuity. Additionally, they cannot have converted their FEGLI coverage to an individual policy.

list.title: Retirement on an immediate annuity:
list.snippet: This means you must be eligible for retirement benefits immediately upon leaving your job.

list.title: Enrollment in FEGLI for five years:
list.snippet: You must have been enrolled in FEGLI for the five years immediately preceding your retirement or for the full period of your federal service if it was less than five years.

list.title: No conversion to individual policy:
list.snippet: You cannot have converted your FEGLI coverage to a private insurance policy.

list.title: Basic Life Insurance:
list.snippet: You can choose to continue your Basic life insurance coverage, and there are different reduction options:
75% Reduction: This is the default option. Your coverage reduces by 2% per month starting at age 65 (or retirement if later) until it reaches 25% of the original amount, according to OPM.
50% Reduction: Your coverage reduces by 1% per month until it reaches 50% of the original amount, according to OPM.
No Reduction: You maintain the same coverage you had as an employee, but you will continue to pay premiums for life, according to OPM.

list.title: Optional Coverage (B and C):
list.snippet: These can also be continued, but with potential reductions or the option to reduce or cancel the coverage.
Accidental Death & Dismemberment (AD&D): AD&D coverage stops at retirement.
Canceling FEGLI: If you cancel your FEGLI coverage in retirement, it cannot be reinstated later.
Conversion to individual policy: If you convert to an individual policy, you will need to apply and pay premiums within 31 days of your retirement, according to FEDweek.

related_questions.question: What does basic life insurance cover?

text_blocks.snippet: Basic life insurance, often provided by employers, typically covers the policyholder's life during the term of employment, providing a death benefit to designated beneficiaries. This benefit is often a multiple of the employee's salary. It is a relatively low-cost option and may not require a medical exam, but the coverage amount may be limited.

list.title: Death benefit:
list.snippet: The primary benefit is a lump-sum payment to the beneficiary upon the policyholder's death.

list.title: Salary-based coverage:
list.snippet: The coverage amount is usually tied to the employee's salary, often one or two times their annual income, according to some insurers.

list.title: Term coverage:
list.snippet: Basic life insurance is typically a term life insurance policy, meaning it covers the employee for a specific period, usually while they are employed by the company.

list.title: Accidental Death & Dismemberment (AD&D) (in some cases):
list.snippet: Some basic life insurance plans also include AD&D, which provides a benefit if the employee dies or is seriously injured due to an accident.

list.title: Financial support for beneficiaries:
list.snippet: The death benefit can be used to cover funeral expenses, outstanding debts, living expenses, and other financial needs of the beneficiaries.

list.title: Limited coverage amount:
list.snippet: The death benefit may not be sufficient to cover all potential financial needs, especially if the employee has significant debts or financial obligations.

list.title: Coverage limitations:
list.snippet: It may not cover certain types of deaths, such as those due to suicide within the first two years of the policy (depending on the policy).

list.title: Not portable:
list.snippet: Basic life insurance is often tied to the employer, meaning coverage may not be easily transferable if the employee changes jobs.

list.title: No cash value:
list.snippet: Unlike some other types of life insurance, basic term life insurance does not build up cash value that can be borrowed against.

list.title: Employer-sponsored:
list.snippet: Basic life insurance is often provided as part of an employee benefits package.

list.title: Cost-effective:
list.snippet: It can be a cost-effective way to provide some level of financial protection for beneficiaries.

list.title: Supplemental coverage:
list.snippet: If the basic coverage is not sufficient, employees may want to consider purchasing supplemental life insurance policies.

related_questions.question: How does employer life insurance work?

text_blocks.snippet: Employer-provided life insurance is a benefit where a company purchases a group life insurance policy for its employees. Typically, the employer pays for a basic amount of coverage, often a multiple of the employee's salary, and employees may have the option to purchase additional coverage. This type of insurance is usually a cost-effective way for employees to get life insurance, as the employer often covers the premiums or a significant portion of them.

list.title: Group Policy:
list.snippet: Employer-sponsored life insurance is a form of group insurance, meaning it covers a group of people (the employees) under one policy.

list.title: Automatic Enrollment:
list.snippet: Many employers automatically enroll employees in a basic life insurance plan upon hire, provided they meet eligibility requirements.

list.title: Coverage Amount:
list.snippet: The coverage amount is often tied to the employee's salary, such as one or two times their annual salary.

list.title: Premium Payment:
list.snippet: Employers may pay the full cost of the basic coverage, or they may share the cost with the employee through payroll deductions.

list.title: Additional Coverage:
list.snippet: Employees can often purchase supplemental life insurance through their employer, which is paid for through payroll deductions.

list.title: No Medical Exam (Typically):
list.snippet: For the basic coverage, employees usually don't need to undergo a medical exam or answer detailed health questions.

list.title: Term Life:
list.snippet: Most employer-sponsored life insurance is term life insurance, meaning it covers the employee for a specific period (usually while employed) and has no cash value.

list.title: Termination Upon Leaving:
list.snippet: Generally, employer-provided life insurance coverage ends when the employee leaves the company.

list.title: Coverage Limits:
list.snippet: The basic coverage provided by employers may not be sufficient for all employees' needs, so consider supplemental insurance or a separate individual policy.

list.title: Tax Implications:
list.snippet: If the employer pays for group life insurance coverage exceeding $50,000, the cost of the excess coverage may be considered taxable income for the employee.

list.title: Continuation Options:
list.snippet: Some policies may allow employees to convert their group policy to an individual policy or continue paying premiums on their own after leaving the company.

list.title: Individual Policy Comparison:
list.snippet: It's wise to compare the cost and benefits of employer-provided life insurance with those of individual policies, especially when considering long-term coverage needs.

text_blocks.snippet: In essence, employer-provided life insurance is a valuable benefit, but it's important to understand its limitations and consider whether additional coverage is necessary.
